3. The certified copy of the order-sheet shows that the defendants entered appearance on 17.5.82 and they were given time to file a written statement many a time until 3.5.83 when the Court fixed 20.6.83 for written statement "in default for ex parte disposal". Thereafter the defendants did not file any written statement nor took any steps and the suit was again fixed for ex parte disposal on 28.7.83 and then on to 31.8.83 and from that date to 15.9.83. In the meantime, the managing director of the plaintiff-company was examined as P.W. 1 on commission. On 14.9.83 the Pleader Commissioner who took down the said evidence on commission submitted his report. On 15.9.83 upon the petitioner's prayer the exhibits/documents were kept in the safe custody of the She restored. No other proceedings are on record. The Court fixed 29.9.83 and later 28.11.83 for passing order. In the meantime, the defendant-opposite parties filed a written statement on 28.11.83 along with a show cause petition with a prayer to accept the written statement. This application was considered by the learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 19.2.84. He described how the defendants defaulted in filing a written statement on several occasions and how they absented themselves from the ex parte proceedings and even from moving the application on 19.2.84. He then rejected the opposite parties' application and fixed 28.3.84 for order. The defendant-opposite parties thereafter filed an application on 28.3.84 for recalling the Court's order dated 19.2.84 and for allowing the defendants to contest the suit after acceptance of their written statement. By the impugned order dated 9.4.84 the learned Subordinate Judge ordered that since no ex parte decree has been passed, the defendants' prayer should be allowed for ends of justice. The written statement was accepted subject to payment of costs of TK. 250/- to the plaintiff-petitioner by 7.5.84. 

 8. Since Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed's submission is based solely on the decision of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Arjun Singh-Vs- Mohindra Kumar and others, A.I.R. 1964 (S.C.) 993, we might as well look into the facts and ratio of the decision very briefly. Of the three suits which were being tried together the appellant before the Supreme Court of India was a defendant in two suits, and plaintiff in one. Written statements were filed, issues, were framed and repeated adjournments were taken on the ground of reaching a compromise. Lastly, no adjournment was granted on the ground of compromise and the three suits were fixed for final hearing on a certain date if no compromise was filed. On the date of hearing the appellant was absent and the other side was present The suit in which the appellant was the plaintiff was dismissed for default. In the 'other two suits' in which the appellant was the defendant, the ex parte hearing was concluded but the judgment was reserved. The appellant prayed for setting aside the ex parte orders and decree, by way of preferring an application, which, in, the absence of a nomenclature, was presumed to be an application under Order 9, role 7 (in the two suits in which the appellant was the defendant) and Order 9, rule 9 (in the suit in which the appellant was the plaintiff). The appellant pleaded illness on the date of hearing, but, by a common judgment the plea, was rejected on merit The ex parte decree was refused to be set aside. The two suits in which judgment was reserved were fixed for delivery of judgment 

 9. The appellant then moved the Allahabad High Court in revision. The High Court disposed of the application by allowing the appellant to participate in the proceedings of the suits reserved for judgment, from the stage on which the suits stood on the date fixed for judgment The appellant then applied to the trial Court to take evidence on his behalf. The trial Court took the view that hearing in the two suits was over and all that the appellant was entitled to was to hear the judgment. In that view of the matter both the two suits in which the appellant was the defendant were decreed, 

 10. The appellant then filed an application under Order 9, rule 13 to set aside the ex parte decree. The same ground of illness was urged. It was held both by the trial Court and the High Court on revision, inter alia that the earlier finding on non-appearance operated as res judicata. Before the Indian Supreme Court the simple question was whether the subsequent application under Order 9,rule 13 on the same ground of illness operated as a res judicata. 

 17. Hearing in default of written statement stands on a separate footing from 'an ex parte hearing under Order 9, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedures and, therefore the Court must of necessity consider whether in the facts and circumstances of a given case any relief can be given to the defendants even though the hearing in default of the written statement has drawn to a close. The hands of the Court in such a situation are not as tightly bound as has been pronounced by the Indian Supreme Court in a case under Order 9 rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Before the decree is passed in a suit fixed for hearing in default of written statement, the defendants may come to the Court and file a written statement and it remains in the domain of the Court's discretionary jurisdiction as to whether the written statement should be accepted or not. The defendants cannot demand the acceptance of the written statement as a matter of right. The court can accept the written statement as a matter of indulgence to the defendants, but whether it will do so or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. If, however, the Court exercises a discretion in favour of the defendants and accepts the written statement after giving reasons there for, the superior Court will not interfere with the reason except when it is perverse, nor will it substitute its own reasoning for the reasoning given by the subordinate Court. If, however a discretion is exercised it is necessary that the Court gives reasons therefor and if no reasons are given it is permissible for the superior Court either to interfere with the decision or to uphold the decision by giving its own reasons.
